main.title: Crazy Climber
main.summary: Crazy Climber is a 1980 action video game developed by Nichibutsu and Jorudan and published by Nichibutsu for arcades.

cards.text: Crazy Climber is a 1980 action video game developed by Nichibutsu and Jorudan and published by Nichibutsu for arcades. In North America, the game was also released by Taito. Ports for the Arcadia 2001 and Atari 2600 were published in 1982, followed by the Famicom in 1986 and X68000 in 1993.

With the goal of scaling a series of skyscrapers using two joysticks (one controlling the left side of the character's body, the other the right) Crazy Climber was the first in a "climbing games" genre which includes Nintendo's 1981 Donkey Kong. The genre eventually became better known as platform games and is defined by jumping and traversal between platforms, neither of which are found in Crazy Climber.

Crazy Climber was the third highest-earning arcade game of 1980 in Japan while also being a commercial success in North America. A lesser-known sequel, Crazy Climber 2, was released for arcades in 1988.

main.title: Missile Command
main.summary: Missile Command is a 1980 shoot 'em up video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades.

cards.text: Missile Command is a 1980 shoot 'em up video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. It was released by Taito and Sega in Japan. The game was designed by Dave Theurer, who would also design Tempest for Atari the following year. The player uses a trackball to defend six cities from intercontinental ballistic missiles by launching anti-ballistic missiles from three bases.

Missile Command was released in June 1980 during the Cold War, where it achieved widespread critical and commercial success. Atari then ported it to home systems beginning with an Atari 2600 conversion in 1981 by Rob Fulop. Numerous clones and modern remakes soon followed, and the version ported to Atari's 8-bit computers was reused for the 5200 in 1982 and built into the XEGS in 1987. It is considered to be one of the greatest video games of all time.

main.title: Berzerk
main.summary: Berzerk is a 1980 maze and shooter video game developed and published by Stern Electronics for arcades.

cards.text: Berzerk is a 1980 maze and shooter video game developed and published by Stern Electronics for arcades. The game involves a Humanoid Intruder who has to escape maze-like rooms that are littered with robots which slowly move toward and shoot at the Humanoid. The player can shoot at the robots to try to escape the room. Along with the robots, a smiley face known as Evil Otto appears to hunt down the player within each room.

The first game to be developed in-house at Stern, Berzerk was designed by programmer Alan McNeil. He slowly developed a game with robots at first, and then later added the walls and the Evil Otto character to expand on the gameplay. After the company was visited by a salesperson promoting a "speech chip", McNeil took the offer and incorporated digitized voices that taunt the player during gameplay and attract mode. Following Stratovox (1980), it was one of the earliest games to use speech synthesis.

Stern premiered the game at the Amusement & Music Operators Association (AMOA) exposition in Chicago in late 1980. It was released shortly thereafter, and sold around 15,000 units. Conversions to the Atari 2600 and Vectrex home consoles were released in 1982, followed by the  Atari 5200 in 1984. They were generally received well by the video game press. The Atari 2600 version received a Certificate of Merit award for "Best Solitaire Videogame" from Electronic Games.

McNeil developed a 1982 sequel, Frenzy, with more variety. Berzerk directly influenced Robotron: 2084 (1982). The game appeared on various "best of" lists and articles from publications like Flux in 1995, GameSpy in 2002, and Retro Gamer in 2008.

main.title: 3-D Tic-Tac-Toe
main.subtitle: Four boards and a line through three dimensions
main.summary: Atari's strategy game places four-in-a-row across a stack of boards, with computer opponents or a second player.

cards.heading: Atari brings the board into three dimensions
cards.text: 3-D Tic-Tac-Toe is Atari's strategy game for the Video Computer System, programmed by Carol Shaw. Four four-by-four boards represent a three-dimensional playing space. Players place crosses or circles, aiming to complete a line of four on a board or through the stack.

cards.heading: Reading a line across four planes
cards.text: The joystick moves a blinking cursor between squares and planes; pressing the button commits a move. Looking across the four boards matters as much as examining one row. A position can contribute to a line running vertically or diagonally through the stack, creating threats on several levels.

cards.heading: Playing a person or the computer
cards.text: Eight settings provide increasingly demanding computer opponents, while a ninth mode supports two human players. Higher settings search further ahead and can take longer to choose a move. At the highest setting, the manual allows up to twenty minutes; the boards temporarily give way to changing colours during calculation.

main.title: Mystery House
main.subtitle: When a Drawn House Changes How an Adventure Is Read
main.summary: Mystery House arrived on Apple II on May 5, 1980.

cards.heading: When a Drawn House Changes How an Adventure Is Read
cards.text: Mystery House is a graphical adventure released for Apple II on 5 May 1980. Roberta Williams designed the mystery and drew its images, while Ken Williams programmed the system. Players type commands and read responses alongside line drawings of the rooms. The game began On-Line Systems' adventure-game business, which later developed under the Sierra name.

cards.heading: Text Meets a Visible Room
cards.text: Players type actions, collect objects and discover which commands the program understands. A line drawing accompanies each room, showing doors, stairs and objects that may be useful. The picture supplies clues about the place, while written commands allow the player to investigate it. Progress depends on connecting something visible with an action the parser can recognise.

cards.heading: Roberta Draws the Mystery by Hand
cards.text: Roberta produced the drawings and designed how discoveries developed through the house. Ken built the tools that displayed those images on Apple II. Memory limits required simple, readable pictures. Their small production combined the design of the mystery, its illustrations and the programming needed to respond to the player's commands.

cards.heading: From the House, Sierra Emerges
cards.text: Mystery House gave the Williamses a direction for their business. On-Line Systems became Sierra, continuing to develop adventures with increasingly visual interfaces and animated characters. Later hardware allowed more elaborate rooms, while images remained part of how players found clues and understood where they were.

main.title: Pac-Man
main.subtitle: PAC-MAN Makes a Maze Readable and Invents a Global Language
main.summary: Toru Iwatani and Namco gave maze-chasing a cast, a personality and a bright visual identity.

cards.heading: A maze chase from Namco
cards.text: Pac-Man, originally titled Puck Man in Japan, is a 1980 maze game developed and published by Namco for arcades. Its first Japanese focus test took place on 22 May, followed by public release in July; Midway brought it to North America in October. Players eat every dot in a maze while avoiding four ghosts. Large Power Pellets temporarily make the ghosts blue and vulnerable, allowing Pac-Man to eat them for bonus points.

cards.heading: Toru Iwatani and a broader audience
cards.text: Pac-Man was designed by Toru Iwatani, who led a nine-man team; the game's development began in early 1979. Iwatani wanted to create a game that could appeal to women as well as men, because most video games of the time had themes that appealed to traditionally masculine interests, such as war or sports. Although the inspiration for the Pac-Man character was the image of a pizza with a slice removed, Iwatani has said he rounded out the Japanese character for mouth, kuchi. The in-game characters were made to be cute and colorful to appeal to younger players. The original Japanese title of Puck Man was derived from the Japanese phrase paku paku taberu, which refers to gobbling something up; the title was changed to Pac-Man for the North American release due to fears of vandals defacing cabinets by converting the P into an F, as in fuck.

cards.heading: Eating every dot in the maze
cards.text: Pac-Man is an action maze chase video game; the player controls the eponymous character through an enclosed maze. The objective of the game is to eat all of the dots placed in the maze while avoiding four colored ghosts—Blinky (red), Pinky (pink), Inky (cyan), and Clyde (orange)—who pursue Pac-Man. When Pac-Man eats all of the dots, the player advances to the next level. Levels are indicated by fruit icons at the bottom of the screen. In between levels are short cutscenes featuring Pac-Man and Blinky in humorous, comical situations.

cards.heading: Four ghosts with different strategies
cards.text: If Pac-Man is caught by a ghost, he loses a life; the game ends when all lives are lost. Each of the four ghosts has its own unique artificial intelligence (A.I.), or "personality": Blinky gives direct chase to Pac-Man; Pinky and Inky try to position themselves in front of Pac-Man, usually by cornering him; and Clyde switches between chasing and fleeing from Pac-Man depending on his distance from him.

cards.heading: When the chase reverses
cards.text: A power pellet temporarily reverses the relationship between hunter and hunted. The maze has not changed, but routes that felt dangerous now become opportunities. Because the advantage expires, confidence carries its own deadline: a decision to chase must include a plan for becoming vulnerable again.

features.title: Starting with a word
features.summary: An invitation took shape through food and movement.

cards.heading: An idea before a circuit
cards.text: Iwatani told Susan Lammers that Pac-Man began with a word: eat. He sketched while considering an arcade game women could enjoy, using a familiar activity in place of the violent themes he associated with existing machines. His interest in images that communicated quickly helped shape both the character and the action around collecting food.

cards.heading: Making the pursuit work
cards.text: Iwatani identified coordinating the four enemies' movements as the hardest part of the design. He called their behaviour the heart of the game. The simple task of eating dots needed opponents whose pursuit produced an engaging challenge. Sketches and diagrams helped him explain those movements as well as the characters' appearance.

cards.heading: Testing before releasing
cards.text: Bandai Namco's official history records a first focus test on 22 May 1980 and Japanese public release in July. Between them, Pac-Man appeared on Shinjuku ALTA's large television screen on 29 June. The dates describe separate stages in testing, presenting and releasing the game.

cards.heading: The image leaves the cabinet
cards.text: The official timeline credits Iwatani with planning, Shigeo Funaki with programming and Toshio Kai with sound. It also follows Pac-Man into a television cartoon and a hit song. Those productions introduced further collaborators, supplying voices, music and situations for a character whose recognisable shape could travel beyond the arcade cabinet.

main.title: Dona Bailey and Centipede
main.subtitle: A new way to move through the arcade
main.summary: Dona Bailey brought programming experience from car electronics to Atari, then helped make a mushroom field feel immediate beneath a player's hand.

cards.heading: From microprocessors to Atari
cards.text: Dona Bailey programmed microprocessors at General Motors before joining Atari's coin-operated games division in 1980. Encountering Space Invaders introduced her to arcade machines using technology she recognised from car electronics. At Atari she would work with Ed Logg on Centipede, applying that programming experience to a game controlled by a trackball.

cards.heading: A field beneath the trackball
cards.text: Centipede grew from a brief idea in Atari's notebook: a segmented insect descending onto the screen. Bailey worked with Ed Logg to turn that premise into the 1981 game. The centipede threaded through mushrooms, while other creatures disrupted the space around the player. The trackball made movement continuous and physical. A quick sweep of the hand could carry the shooter across the bottom of the screen.

cards.heading: An invitation to more players
cards.text: Bailey wanted the game to look appealing in a dark arcade and its controls to feel approachable. The familiar insects, changing colours and direct movement gave it a character of its own. She has described hoping that everyone would enjoy it, rather than designing it only for a particular gender.

cards.heading: Restoring the programmer to the story
cards.text: Bailey's later interviews describe being the only woman software engineer in Atari's coin-operated division. Alongside discussing Centipede's design and controls, she recalled the isolation of that position. Her account records both the programming decisions behind the game and her experience of the workplace in which it was developed.

features.title: Making Centipede ready for people
features.summary: Making, testing and teaching an arcade game.

cards.heading: The invisible parts of an arcade game
cards.text: A descending insect was only the start of Centipede's development. In her Arcade Attack interview, Dona Bailey describes beginning with an existing hardware board already proved dependable. Graphics, play, scoring and sound arrived in stages. Other work would rarely be visible to a visitor watching a single game: test facilities, an attract sequence, coin handling and support for the cocktail cabinet. These were part of making an arcade product. The program had to behave usefully before someone paid, during a contest and when a technician examined it.

cards.heading: Letting unfamiliar players try
cards.text: Bailey's account places a focus group and arcade testing before the production line began shipping machines in May 1981. Those encounters gave the team something different from its own familiarity with the game. She describes wanting an appealing, shimmering display and a trackball people would enjoy using, while resisting the assumption that she designed only for women. The intended invitation was broader. Visual pleasure and accessible movement were choices about how a person might approach the machine, rather than decoration after its rules were finished.

cards.heading: Programming as a language
cards.text: In her 2007 interview with Leigh Alexander, Bailey described programming through syntax, structure and rules. She had enjoyed reading and writing before learning to code. Assembly language gave her another way to organise an image or interaction, extending her earlier work with microprocessors into the different problems of making an arcade game.

cards.heading: Making tools reachable
cards.text: By 2007, Bailey was teaching writing and multimedia in Arkansas. She identified the price of professional software as an obstacle for students and welcomed free tools such as Blender. Her teaching returned to a practical difficulty she remembered from entering game development: obtaining the information and equipment needed to learn.

main.title: Centipede
main.summary: Centipede is a 1981 fixed shooter video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades.

cards.text: Centipede is a 1981 fixed shooter video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for arcades. Designed by Dona Bailey and Ed Logg, it was one of the most commercially successful games from the golden age of arcade video games, and one of the first widely played by women and girls. The primary objective is to shoot all the segments of a centipede that winds down the playing field.

Centipede was ported to Atari's own 2600, 5200, 7800, and 8-bit computers. Under the Atarisoft label, the game was sold for the Apple II, Commodore 64, ColecoVision, VIC-20, IBM PC (as a self-booting disk), Intellivision, and TI-99/4A. Superior Software published the port for the BBC Micro. Versions for the Game Boy and Game Boy Color were also produced, as well as a version for the short-lived Game.com. Other developers released more than 25 Centipede clones for home computers. It was followed by the arcade sequel Millipede in 1982. In 1998, a 3D remake for Windows, Mac, PlayStation, and Dreamcast was published by Hasbro Interactive.

main.title: Defender
main.summary: Defender is a horizontally scrolling shooter video game developed and published by Williams Electronics for arcades in 1981.

cards.text: Defender is a horizontally scrolling shooter developed and published by Williams Electronics for arcades in 1981. The player pilots a spaceship over a mountainous planet, fighting waves of invading aliens with different behaviours. Attacking the enemies is only part of the task: astronauts on the surface must also be protected and rescued.

A pinball developer at the time, Williams aimed to expand into video games and selected Eugene Jarvis to lead development. The development team initially focused on designing the game's arcade hardware, aiming to portray Williams as a technologically advanced developer. When creating early prototypes, Jarvis drew inspiration from Space Invaders and Asteroids. He progressively added offensive and defensive action to the game design, which culminated in gameplay that was more complex and challenging than contemporary video games.

Defender debuted at trade shows in late 1980 before releasing to arcades in March 1981. Williams licensed it to local video game companies in Japan and the United Kingdom when exporting overseas, eventually selling 70,000 units worldwide. The company registered copyrights and trademarks related to Defender, which it used to litigate companies that produced unauthorized clones and copies. Ports were developed for contemporary game systems by either Atari, Inc. or its software label for non-Atari platforms, Atarisoft. Midway Games handled many of the later ports and re-releases. Defender was followed by sequels and remade in different formats.

The game was commercially successful, becoming one of the highest-grossing arcade games. It quickly increased Williams net income and eventually earned the company US$1 billion. Defender's challenging gameplay and complex control scheme were frequently discussed in contemporary commentary. The ports met with varying degrees of mixed reception. The 1982 Atari 2600 version was one of the best-selling games for the system, selling over 3 million cartridges. Retrospective reviews frequently rank Defender among the top video games, citing its innovative and challenging gameplay. It is often listed as one of Jarvis's best contributions and cited as the inspiration for other games as well as several songs.

main.title: Qix
main.summary: Qix is a 1981 arcade puzzle game developed and published by Taito.

cards.text: Qix is a 1981 arcade puzzle game developed and published by Taito. Randy and Sandy Pfeiffer designed it within the company's American division. The player draws lines to close off and fill sections of a large rectangle. Inside it, the Qix moves unpredictably as an abstract figure of shifting lines. Each level asks the player to capture a required proportion of the field.

Qix was ported to the contemporary Atari 5200 (1982), Atari 8-bit computers (1983), and Commodore 64 (1983), then was brought to a wide variety of systems in the late 1980s and early 1990s: MS-DOS (1989), Amiga (1989), another version for the C64 (1989), Apple IIGS (1990), Game Boy (1990), Nintendo Entertainment System (1991), and Atari Lynx (1991).

Multiple home and arcade sequels followed and the concept was widely cloned. In the Gals Panic series from Kaneko, each captured area is not filled with a color, but reveals part of an image of a woman; this itself has been cloned into erotic-oriented games based on the concept of Qix.
